\chapter{Hablamos --- We Speak, and We Spoke}
\label{ch:hablamos-dos}
\hlchaptermodality{200}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use one form for both tenses and let context decide.}

I can use one form for both tenses and let context decide.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablamos]{hablamos}

\label{lesson:ES-C55-hablamos-dos}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}we speak.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hablamos}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}they spoke.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hablaron}.)

Now say \textquotedblleft{}we spoke.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the form you already own}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{hablamos}} — we speak \textbf{and} we spoke.
\end{quote}

There is nothing to learn. For every \textbf{regular} \emph{-ar} verb the \emph{we} form is \textbf{identical} in the present and the past:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{past} \\
\midrule
\emph{nosotros} & \textbf{hablamos} & \textbf{hablamos} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Latin kept them apart — \emph{-āmus} for now, \emph{-āvimus} for then — and the second one wore down until it landed on top of the first. Spanish noticed, and did nothing about it.

\textbf{Context does the work instead}, exactly as it does in English \emph{I put it there}, where \emph{put} is present or past and nobody is ever confused.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{A gap that costs nothing is a gap a language keeps.}

Spanish could have invented a new ending. It did not, because the two meanings almost never compete: whatever else is in the sentence — a time word, the verb before it, the conversation you are already in — settles which one you meant.

And when it genuinely matters, a speaker just says when. That is cheaper than a new tense form for every verb in the language.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hablamos} — meaning now
  \item \emph{hablamos} — meaning then
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many new forms did this chapter cost you? (\textbf{None}.)

What tells a listener which tense you meant? (\textbf{Context} — and if it matters, you say when.)
\end{tcolorbox}
